brief:
Translate the given UI strings from English into ko for a software product.
These strings describe what a design-tool web app called Lolly can do — they are the feature map on its dashboard. Unlike button labels, many are full explanatory sentences or short paragraphs written for a curious professional (a designer, a print operator, a developer). Translate them as clear, confident product prose in the target language — same length, same register, no marketing embellishment and no added explanation. Several contain authored inline HTML (<code>, <strong>, <em>, <a href="…">): keep every tag, attribute and entity exactly as it appears and translate only the human text around and inside it. Never translate what sits inside a <code> tag (they are literal parameters, flags and file formats), nor format/technology names (PNG, SVG, PDF, CMYK, C2PA, MCP, OAuth 2.1, Tauri, HarfBuzz, IndexedDB, AES-256).
Register: polite standard speech (해요체) — friendly but respectful UI register, the modern SaaS/app default; not deferential formal speech (하십시오체) and not casual banmal (반말).
Never translate these terms — copy them verbatim wherever they appear: "Lolly", "SUSE", "Geeko", "Content Credentials", "C2PA", "Pose Geeko", "Neurospicy".
Preserve every {placeholder} token exactly (same braces, same name, same count) — these are runtime interpolations, not prose.
Preserve any inline HTML exactly: the same tags, the same count, every attribute (href, target, rel) byte-for-byte, and every HTML entity (&, <). Translate only the human text around and between the tags — never a tag name, an attribute value, or the contents of a <code> element.
Preserve punctuation choices like → and & as-is where they read naturally in the target language; do not add explanatory text.
Match the source length and register. Do not pad or embellish.
Return ONLY the JSON matching the given schema — one translation per input id, in the same order.

items.text: No model, no server and no randomness in the render path — outputs are inspectable and version-controllable.
Creative production stays on the device, under your control — rendering, storage and export never require a server. The optional hosted add-ons are listed separately.
No analytics, no telemetry, and rendering happens locally — what you create is stored on your machine, not on a server.

The shells render, export and store everything on-device — no server-side render pipeline, no database. Deploy on your own infrastructure and run entirely behind your firewall; the optional hosted add-ons (the MCP endpoint, identity enrolment) are separate opt-in services you can omit.
When work does leave the device — a share link, a download, a PDF — you decide who can open it. Every lock is applied on-device, and passwords and keys are never sent to a server.

Any share link can be encrypted: the design is AES-256-GCM-encrypted under a key stretched from the password with PBKDF2-SHA256 (210k iterations). The link carries only the ciphertext — opening it prompts the recipient for the password and rebuilds the design in their browser. The password never travels in the link and never reaches a server — the server sees only ciphertext in the URL, and decryption happens entirely in the recipient’s browser.

A tool’s optional logic is written against the host.* bridge — the supported, portable API for storage, network and export — and its calls are time-boxed. This is a portability contract, not an isolation boundary: every tool in the catalogue is first-party and reviewed before it ships, and stronger Worker-based isolation is on the roadmap.

host.net is the sanctioned network path for tools, allowlisted per the tool’s manifest, and tool templates are logic-less with escaping on by default. Network use outside the allowlist is a review failure, caught before a tool ships.
